title: When walking in nature is not restorative—The role of prospect and refuge
research_question: To examine how the physical structure of a natural environment (specifically prospect and refuge) may enhance or reduce actual and perceived restoration, and whether prospect-refuge affects perceived restoration by affecting perceptions of danger and fear.

participants.description: Study 1: 269 respondents (198 female; M=22.48 years, SD=7.84 years; 18-27 years), students and alumni. Study 2: 34 students (17 field, 17 lab; 20 female; M=22.03 years, SD=6.75 years; 18-43 years).
participants.recruitment: Study 1: snowball sampling through social networking websites. Study 2: course credits.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Study 1: 36 photographs (12 per condition) taken in a country park, depicting low, medium, and high prospect-refuge conditions. Presented as a slideshow with a short descriptive text.

Study 2: Two 10-minute first-person perspective videos (with audio) of actual walks in a country park, representing high prospect-low refuge and low prospect-high refuge conditions. Lab condition: projected onto a 307cm x 230cm wall. Field condition: actual walks in the park.

measures.instrument: A&D UA-767 digital blood pressure and heart rate monitor

findings.mechanism: Environments with less clear visibility and more hiding places are perceived as more dangerous.
findings.quote: The difference in perceived danger ratings between the medium and high prospect-low refuge conditions was also found to be significant but statistically weaker than the other two comparisons (t (266) = 2.16, p <.03, d = .26).

findings.quote: Fear ratings from the low prospect-high refuge condition were significantly greater than for those from both the medium prospect-refuge condition (t (172.02) = 4.31, p< .001, d = .66)

findings.mechanism: Environments perceived as more dangerous or fear-inducing are less restorative.
findings.quote: Perceived restoration ratings were significantly lower in the low prospect-high refuge condition than in the medium prospect-refuge condition (t (266) = 5.67, p< .001, d = .70)

findings.mechanism: Environments perceived as more dangerous or fear-inducing are less restorative.
findings.quote: and the high prospect-low refuge condition (t (266) = 8.24, p<.001, d = 1.24).

findings.quote: Perceived restoration ratings from the high prospect-low refuge condition were also significantly greater than those from the medium prospect-refuge condition (t (266) = 2.65, p<.01, d = .32).
Overall prospect-refuge was significantly related to perceived restoration (B = 1.04, error B = .13, p < .001, adj R² = .20, F(1,267) = 69.13, p < .001).
Simple regression analyses also revealed that prospect-refuge was a significant predictor of perceived danger (B = -.48, error B = .099, p < .001)

findings.mechanism: Perception of danger creates stress, disrupting restoration.
findings.quote: and that perceptions of danger significantly explained perceived restoration (B = -.90, error B = .06, p < .001).

findings.mechanism: The link between prospect-refuge and perceived restoration is partially mediated by perceived danger.
findings.quote: The extent to which prospect-refuge predicted perceived restoration was significantly reduced when controlled for the mediating effect of perceived danger (B = .66, error B = .10, Sobel z = 4.55, p < .01).
Prospect-refuge significantly predicted fear (B = -1.09, error B = .16, p < .001)

findings.mechanism: Feelings of fear create stress, disrupting restoration.
findings.quote: and fear significantly explained perceived restoration (B = -.68, error B = .03, p < .001).

findings.mechanism: The link between prospect-refuge and perceived restoration is partially mediated by fear.
findings.quote: this relationship was significantly reduced when controlled for the mediating effect of fear (B = .34, error B = .08, Sobel z = 6.56, p < .001).

findings.mechanism: Environments with clear views and few hiding places are more restorative for positive affect.
findings.quote: Restoration of positive affect was significantly greater following the walks through the high prospect-low refuge environments (M = 2.50) than the low prospect-high refuge environments (M = 1.36; F (1, 66) = 47.78, p<.001, d = 1.72).

findings.mechanism: Simulated walks may be perceived as less demanding or threatening than real walks, leading to greater self-reported restoration.
findings.quote: On average, the field walks (M = 1.53) were significantly less restorative than the simulated laboratory walks (M = 2.33; F (1, 66) = 7.76, p<.01, d = 0.68).

findings.mechanism: Environments perceived as less safe or more threatening can increase negative mood states like sadness.
findings.quote: In high prospect-low refuge environments sadness slightly decreased (M = -0.03) but in the low prospect-high refuge environments it increased (M = 1.04). A significant interaction effect was found between walk type and environment (F (1, 66) = 10.66, p<.001).

findings.mechanism: Real-world exposure to safe, open natural environments is highly effective in reducing negative mood.
findings.quote: A significant interaction effect was found between walk type and environment (F (1, 66) = 10.66, p<.001). Figure 3 shows that the reduction of sadness was particularly strong in the high prospect-low refuge field walk.

findings.antecedent: low prospect-high refuge environment (field and lab)
findings.mechanism: Environments perceived as less safe or more threatening can increase negative mood states like sadness.
findings.quote: The increase in sadness ratings for those exposed to the low prospect-high refuge environments were also found to be significant for both field and laboratory conditions (all p's<.03).

findings.mechanism: Open, non-threatening environments allow for involuntary attention, restoring directed attention capacity.
findings.quote: Restoration of attentiveness was significantly greater following the walk through the high prospect-low refuge environments (M = 1.00) than the low prospect-high refuge environments which actually recorded a reduction in attentiveness ratings (M = -0.22; F (1, 66) = 59.22, p<.001, d = 1.92).

findings.mechanism: Environments requiring directed attention to navigate or avoid threats can further deplete attentional capacity.
findings.quote: Attentiveness ratings increased significantly for those taking the high prospect-low refuge walks (p's<.01), but not for those taking the low prospect-high refuge walks (p's>.05).

findings.mechanism: Real-world exposure to safe, open natural environments is highly effective in restoring attentiveness.
findings.quote: However a significant interaction effect was found (F (1, 66) = 12.07, p<.001). Figure 3 shows that the increase in attentiveness in the high prospect-low refuge conditions and the decrease in attentiveness in the low prospect-high refuge conditions was particularly strong in the field conditions.

findings.mechanism: Environments with clear views and few hiding places reduce perceived threat and fear.
findings.quote: Fear arousal went down among participants exposed to the high prospect-low refuge walks (M = -0.52) but it went up in the low prospect-high refuge walks (M = 0.25; F(1, 66) = 23.72, p<.001, d = 1.18).

findings.mechanism: Real-world exposure to dense, enclosed environments with many hiding places can increase fear.
findings.quote: A significant decrease in fear arousal ratings was found for both high prospect-low refuge walks (p's<.001) and a significant increase in fear arousal in the low prospect-high refuge field walk (p<.001) but not in the low prospect-high refuge lab walk.

findings.mechanism: Environments with clear views and few hiding places reduce negative emotional states.
findings.quote: Finally anger/aggression ratings reduced for those exposed to the high prospect-low refuge walks (M = -1.16) while it increased for those who took the low prospect-high refuge walks (M = 0.25; F (1, 66) = 56.72, p<.001, d = 1.94).

findings.mechanism: Real-world experiences may have a stronger impact on emotional regulation than simulated ones.
findings.quote: Moreover, the field walks resulted in a reduction in anger/aggression (M = -1.27) but not the laboratory walks (M = 0.25; F (1, 66) = 19.32, p<.001, d = 1.07).

findings.mechanism: Real-world exposure to safe, open natural environments is highly effective in reducing anger/aggression.
findings.quote: Restoration appeared greatest in the high prospect-low refuge field walk (see Figure 3). Anger/aggression decreased significantly in both high prospect-low refuge walks (p's<.001) but increases in the low prospect-high refuge walks were not significant (p's>.05).

findings.mechanism: Open, non-threatening environments allow for involuntary attention, restoring directed attention capacity and improving concentration.
findings.quote: NCPCT scores reduced following the walks through the high prospect-low refuge environments (M = -0.42) but increased after walks through the low prospect-high refuge environments (M = 0.61; F (1, 66) = 8.74, p<.01, d = 4.79, see Figure 4).

findings.mechanism: Environments requiring directed attention to navigate or avoid threats can further deplete attentional capacity, worsening concentration.
findings.quote: NCPCT scores reduced following the walks through the high prospect-low refuge environments (M = -0.42) but increased after walks through the low prospect-high refuge environments (M = 0.61; F (1, 66) = 8.74, p<.01, d = 4.79, see Figure 4).

findings.mechanism: Real-world experiences provide more sensory information and engagement, leading to greater cognitive restoration than simulations.
findings.quote: Cognitive restoration was also greater in the field walks (M = -0.10) than in the simulated laboratory walks (M = 0.28; F (1, 66) = 5.85, p<.001, d = 1.77).

findings.mechanism: The combination of a restorative environment and real-world experience leads to the strongest cognitive restoration.
findings.quote: Moreover, environment and walk type were found to significantly interact (F (1, 66) = 9.15, p<.01). Tukey HSD post-hocs showed that improvements in ability to 'hold' the cube patterns were significantly greater in the high prospect-low refuge field condition than the other three conditions (all p's<.01).

findings.mechanism: Environments perceived as safe and non-threatening promote physiological relaxation.
findings.quote: Reductions in heart rate were significantly greater following the walk through the high prospect-low refuge environments (M = 8.33) than the low prospect-high refuge environments (M = 3.43; F (1, 66) = 12.83, p<.001, d = 0.88).

findings.mechanism: Sitting still in a lab does not increase heart rate due to physical activity, allowing for clearer observation of physiological restoration.
findings.quote: The change in heart rate in the field walks (M = 3.00) was significantly smaller than the change in heart rate in the laboratory walks (M = 8.26; F (1, 66) = 15.02, p<.001, d = 0.94), suggesting that the laboratory walk was more restorative.

findings.mechanism: The combination of a restorative environment and the absence of physical exertion in a lab setting leads to the greatest physiological relaxation.
findings.quote: Post-hoc tests showed that reductions in heart rate in the high prospect-low refuge laboratory condition are significantly greater than in the other three conditions (all p's<.01).

mechanisms: Environments with high prospect and low refuge are perceived as less dangerous and evoke less fear, which in turn promotes restoration by reducing stress and allowing for involuntary attention.

Environments with low prospect and high refuge demand more directed attention to navigate or look out for threats, disrupting the restoration process and potentially increasing stress and attention fatigue.
Physical activity (walking in the field) can confound physiological measures of restoration (e.g., heart rate) compared to passive exposure (simulated lab walks).
moderators: Walk type (field vs. simulated laboratory experience)
implementation_implications: Design and manage country parks to contain a high degree of prospect and accessibility but a low number of hiding places to maximize restorative benefits.

Environmental planners and designers should consider Fisher and Nasar's (1992) typology of prospect-refuge when designing and maintaining natural environments, especially wooded areas in country parks.

tables.description: Mean ratings (standard deviation) and ANOVA for prospect, accessibility and hiding places across the three prospect-refuge conditions.
Mean danger, fear and restoration ratings (standard deviation) for the three prospect-refuge conditions.

limitations: Studies were entirely based on student samples, limiting generalisability to other populations (e.g., age, gender).
Examined only relatively short-term effects of exposure to environments and short cognitive depletion manipulation.
Did not examine the role of company in nature experiences, which can affect perceived safety and restoration.
Use of images/simulations raises questions about ecological validity, as they exclude sensory experiences and prevent movement.
Blood pressure data was deemed unreliable due to potential exogenous variables and infrequent measurement.
Research did not allow for separation of effects for prospect and refuge, only combined effects.
Did not include examples of very open environments with very high levels of prospect and no refuge.
Did not explore a curvilinear relationship between prospect-refuge and restoration.
